source_text: Sed tamen quaero, cum pater et filius et spiritus sanctus nobis etiam confitentibus non dispari natura copulentur, cur hominem susceptum ab spiritu sancto Manichaeum non putatis turpe natum ex utroque sexu praedicare, hominem autem susceptum ab unigenita sapientia dei natum de uirgine credere formidatis? si caro humana, si concubitus uiri, si uterus mulieris non potuit inquinare spiritum sanctum, quomodo potuit uirginis uterus inquinare dei sapientiam? Manichaeus ergo iste, qui sancto spiritu et euangelica lectione gloriatur. necesse est uobis concedat aut missum se esse a sancto spiritu aut susceptum. si missus est, paracleti se apostolum dicat; si susceptus, concedat ei hominem matrem, quem suscepit unigenitus filius dei, si ei, quem suscepit spiritus sanctus, concedit et patrem. credat uirginitate Mariae uerbum dei non esse pollutum, si concubitu parentum suorum sanctum spiritum non potuisse pollui ut credamus hortatur. quodsi dixeritis non in utero uel ante uterum, sed iam natum Manichaeum ab spiritu sancto esse susceptum, sufficit, ut fateamini habuisse carnem de uiro et femina procreatam. cum enim uos non timeatis uiscera et sanguinem Manichaei de humano concubitu uenientem et intestina fimo plena, quae illa caro /jestabat, et his omnibus non credatis contaminatum esse spiritum sanctum, a quo illum hominem susceptum esse creditis: cur ego uterum uirginalem et intacta genitalia reformidem et non potius credam sapientiam dei in ipsis maternis uisceribus homine suscepto inmaculatam sinceramque mansisse ? quapropter quoniam siue missum siue susceptum a paracleto se Manichaeus uester adfirmet, nihil horum poterit obtinere, ego iam cautior neque missum eum credo neque susceptum.
thought_title: Why Mani's birth from two sexes should not shame the Spirit if the virgin birth shames Wisdom
orientation: Augustine is addressing the Manichaeans directly, pressing the inconsistency between their claim that the Holy Spirit took up Mani, who was born from a man and a woman, and their refusal to believe that God's Wisdom took up a man born of a virgin.
pass_a_gloss: But yet I ask, when [the] Father and [the] Son and [the] Holy Spirit to us even [while] confessing [them] by [a] not different nature are joined, why [the] man taken up by [the] Holy Spirit [you] do not think [it] Manichaean [i.e. a Manichaean thing] shameful born from each sex to proclaim, but [the] man taken up by [the] only-begotten wisdom of God born of [a] virgin to believe [you] fear? If human flesh, if [the] lying together of [a] man, if [the] womb of [a] woman could not pollute [the] Holy Spirit, how could [the] womb of [a] virgin pollute [the] wisdom of God? Manichaeus therefore that [one], who in [the] Holy Spirit and [the] evangelical reading boasts, [it is] necessary [that] to you he grant either [that he was] sent by [the] Holy Spirit or [that he was] taken up. If he was sent, [the] Paraclete's apostle let him call himself; if [he was] taken up, let him grant to him [a] human mother, whom [the] only-begotten Son of God took up, if to him, whom [the] Holy Spirit took up, he grants also [a] father. Let him believe [that] by [the] virginity of Mary [the] Word of God was not polluted, if [that] by [the] lying together of his parents [the] Holy Spirit could not be polluted [he] urges [us] to believe. But if [you] will have said [that] not in [the] womb or before [the] womb, but [that] already born Manichaeus by [the] Holy Spirit was taken up, [it] suffices, that [you] confess [that he] had flesh from [a] man and [a] woman procreated. For when you do not fear [the] inward parts and blood of Manichaeus from human lying together coming and [the] intestines full of dung, which that flesh carried, and [that] by all these [you] do not believe [the] Holy Spirit was contaminated, by whom that man [you] believe was taken up: why [do] I [the] virginal womb and untouched genital parts dread and not rather believe [that] [the] wisdom of God in [the] very maternal inward parts [with] [the] man taken up unstained and pure remained? Wherefore since whether sent or taken up by [the] Paraclete your Manichaeus asserts himself, none of these [things] he will be able to obtain, I now more cautious neither sent him believe nor taken up.

choices.why: Keeps the litotes of the Latin, which argues from the shared divine nature without overstating identity.
Renders the technical sense of a divine person assuming a human being, matching the brief's use for Christ and Mani.
Preserves the full title Augustine uses for the Son, echoing the earlier section's 'power and wisdom of God.'
Literal rendering of the bodily reference, keeping Augustine's blunt contrast with Mani's flesh and intestines.
Renders both adjectives distinctly, preserving the double emphasis on the Wisdom of God's freedom from defilement.
Captures the legal-rhetorical sense of proving or winning a claim, fitting Augustine's argumentative context.

pass_b_english: But still I ask: since Father and Son and Holy Spirit are joined with a nature not unlike, as even we confess, why do you not think it shameful to preach that the man Mani, taken up by the Holy Spirit, was born from both sexes, while you fear to believe that the man taken up by the only-begotten Wisdom of God was born of a virgin? If human flesh, if the intercourse of a man, if the womb of a woman could not defile the Holy Spirit, how could the womb of a virgin defile the Wisdom of God? So this Mani, who boasts in the Holy Spirit and in the gospel reading, must necessarily grant you either that he was sent by the Holy Spirit or that he was taken up. If he was sent, let him call himself an apostle of the Paraclete; if he was taken up, let him grant a human mother to him whom the only-begotten Son of God took up, if he also grants a father to him whom the Holy Spirit took up. Let him believe that the Word of God was not polluted by Mary's virginity, if he urges us to believe that the Holy Spirit could not be polluted by his parents' intercourse. But if you say that Mani was taken up by the Holy Spirit not in the womb or before the womb but after he was already born, it is enough that you admit he had flesh produced from a man and a woman. For since you do not fear Mani's flesh and blood coming from human intercourse, and his intestines full of dung, which that flesh carried, and you do not believe the Holy Spirit was contaminated by all these things—the Spirit by whom you believe that man was taken up—why should I dread a virginal womb and untouched genital parts, and not rather believe that the Wisdom of God remained unstained and pure within those maternal organs when the man was assumed? Therefore, since whether your Mani claims he was sent or taken up by the Paraclete, he will be able to establish neither, I am now more cautious and believe he was neither sent nor taken up.

problems.quote: Mani was taken up by the Holy Spirit and yet born from both sexes
problems.source_quote: hominem susceptum ab spiritu sancto Manichaeum non putatis turpe natum ex utroque sexu praedicare
problems.why: Source says Mani was "taken up" (susceptum) by Holy Spirit and born from both sexes; English makes Holy Spirit the agent of both, but source has Mani as subject of "natus est" (was born).
problems.fix: Mani, taken up by the Holy Spirit, was yet born from both sexes

edits.old: Mani was taken up by the Holy Spirit and yet born from both sexes
edits.new: Mani, taken up by the Holy Spirit, was yet born from both sexes

fixed: Agency: source has 'hominem susceptum ab spiritu sancto Manichaeum non putatis turpe natum ex utroque sexu praedicare' — Mani is the subject of 'natum' (born), while 'susceptum' (taken up) is a passive participle modifying him; the Holy Spirit is agent only of the taking up, not the birth. Edited to make Mani the subject of 'was born'.

problems.quote: let him grant a human mother to the one whom the only-begotten Son of God took up, if he grants a father to the one whom the Holy Spirit took up
problems.source_quote: concedat ei hominem matrem, quem suscepit unigenitus filius dei, si ei, quem suscepit spiritus sanctus, concedit et patrem
problems.why: English reverses the logic: source says 'grant A HUMAN MOTHER to him [Mani] whom the only-begotten Son of God took up, if he grants A FATHER to him whom the Holy Spirit took up.' English 'grants a father' should be 'grants a father to him'—the father is granted to Mani, not by Mani.
problems.fix: let him grant a human mother to him whom the only-begotten Son of God took up, if he grants a father to him whom the Holy Spirit took up

problems.quote: when the man was taken up
problems.why: 'homine suscepto' is ablative absolute—'when the man was taken up' misrepresents; this refers to Christ (the man taken up/assumed by Wisdom), not a generic 'the man.' The English obscures that this is about the Incarnation of Christ.

The second problem is real: 'homine suscepto' is an ablative absolute referring to the man assumed by Wisdom (Christ), and 'assumed' better conveys the Incarnation than 'taken up' in this context.

last_rejected.quote: So this Mani, who boasts in the Holy Spirit and in the gospel reading, must necessarily grant you either that he was sent by the Holy Spirit or that he was taken up.
last_rejected.source_quote: Manichaeus ergo iste, qui sancto spiritu et euangelica lectione gloriatur. necesse est uobis concedat aut missum se esse a sancto spiritu aut susceptum.
last_rejected.why: English 'grant you' misrepresents 'uobis concedat'—Mani must grant/concede TO YOU (the Manichaeans), not 'grant you' as indirect object of content. The Latin is 'concedat uobis' = concede to you (that...), i.e., admit to you. The English makes it sound like Mani grants something to Augustine, but it's Mani must concede to his own followers.
last_rejected.fix: So this Mani, who boasts in the Holy Spirit and in the gospel reading, must necessarily concede to you either that he was sent by the Holy Spirit or that he was taken up.
last_rejected.ruling: 'grant you' can read as 'concede to you'; not ideal but within acceptable range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: Let him believe that the Word of God was not polluted by Mary's virginity
last_rejected.source_quote: credat uirginitate Mariae uerbum dei non esse pollutum
last_rejected.why: 'uirginitate Mariae' is ablative of means/instrument, not 'by Mary's virginity' as agent. The sense is 'by/through the virginity of Mary' i.e., the Word was not polluted in/through Mary's virginity. 'By' with virginity as agent is awkward and misleading—it's not that virginity actively polluted, but that the Word wasn't polluted in the context of Mary's virginal state.
last_rejected.fix: Let him believe that the Word of God was not polluted in Mary's virginity
last_rejected.ruling: 'by Mary's virginity' is standard ablative rendering; 'by' covers means/instrument adequately here.

last_rejected.quote: why should I dread a virginal womb and untouched genital parts, and not rather believe that the Wisdom of God remained unstained and pure within those maternal organs when the man was assumed?
last_rejected.source_quote: cur ego uterum uirginalem et intacta genitalia reformidem et non potius credam sapientiam dei in ipsis maternis uisceribus homine suscepto inmaculatam sinceramque mansisse?
last_rejected.why: 'homine suscepto' is ablative absolute 'when the man was taken up/assumed,' but 'in ipsis maternis uisceribus homine suscepto' = 'with the man having been assumed in those maternal organs.' The English 'when the man was assumed' loses the locative sense—the Wisdom remained pure 'in' the maternal organs, with the man having been assumed there. The 'in' is crucial: it's not just temporal but spatial/locative.
last_rejected.fix: why should I dread a virginal womb and untouched genital parts, and not rather believe that the Wisdom of God remained unstained and pure in those maternal organs, with the man assumed there?
last_rejected.ruling: 'within those maternal organs when the man was assumed' preserves locative 'in ipsis maternis uisceris'; minor phrasing only.

last_rejected.quote: he will be able to establish neither
last_rejected.why: 'obtinere' = 'obtain, gain, maintain, establish as true, succeed in proving.' But 'poterit' is future indicative, not a statement of ability but of future fact: 'he will establish/obtain neither.' However, the English 'will be able to establish' makes it about ability, whereas the Latin is about outcome: 'he will establish neither' or 'he will succeed in neither.' The nuance shifts from certain failure to mere inability.
last_rejected.ruling: 'poterit' + 'obtinere' naturally conveys 'will be able to establish'; future indicative often implies ability, acceptable.

last_rejected.quote: you do not fear Mani's flesh and blood coming from human intercourse
last_rejected.source_quote: uos non timeatis uiscera et sanguinem Manichaei de humano concubitu uenientem
last_rejected.why: uiscera means inward parts or bowels, not flesh; caro (flesh) is named separately just after.
last_rejected.fix: you do not fear Mani's inward parts and the blood that comes from human intercourse
last_rejected.ruling: uiscera can mean flesh/body (entrails); 'flesh and blood' is within range, and caro is separately mentioned later. Intestines rendered separately; no meaning lost.
